Pregnancy nausea
Nausea and vomiting affect most pregnant women and usually ease between weeks 12 and 16.
Morning sickness can happen at any time of day.
Hyperemesis gravidarum: severe vomiting causing weight and fluid loss; it needs treatment.
Try not to go hungry; eat small amounts often.
Avoid fatty and strong-smelling foods; cold foods may be easier to tolerate.
Ginger may help some pregnant women; ask your doctor about supplements.
Not keeping anything down for more than 24 hours, less urine, dizziness.
Weight loss, vomiting blood or tummy pain.
Nutrition in pregnancy
In pregnancy it's not about eating "for two" but eating well for two.
Extra energy needs are very small in the first trimester and rise by about 300–450 kcal a day later on.
Caffeine should not exceed 200 mg a day (about 2 cups of filter coffee).
Raw meat, raw eggs, unpasteurised milk and cheese, and raw seafood carry a risk of listeria and toxoplasmosis.
Large fish high in mercury (shark, swordfish) should be limited.
Prepare balanced meals with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes and enough protein.
Wash fruit and vegetables well; cook meat thoroughly.
Two portions a week of low-mercury fish (salmon, sea bass, anchovies) are fine.
No amount of alcohol is safe.
Excessive weight gain or not gaining weight.
Signs of iron deficiency: weakness, paleness, palpitations.
Weight gain in pregnancy
Recommended weight gain depends on your pre-pregnancy body mass index.
For women of normal weight, a total of 11.5–16 kg is usually recommended.
Less is recommended if you start overweight, more if you start underweight.
Sudden weight gain and swelling can be a sign of pre-eclampsia.
Weigh yourself once a week at the same time and record it in the app's pregnancy journal.
Don't diet; control portions with quality foods.
A sudden gain of more than 1 kg in a week together with swelling.
Losing weight or not gaining at all.
Exercise in pregnancy
If there are no risks, regular exercise in pregnancy benefits mother and baby.
A total of 150 minutes of moderate activity a week is recommended.
Exercise can lower the risk of gestational diabetes and ease back pain.
Sports with a risk of falls or blows, and movements that require lying on your back for a long time, are not recommended.
Walking, swimming, a stationary bike and pregnancy yoga are safe choices.
Keep a pace at which you can still talk; drink plenty of water and avoid overheating.
Start pelvic floor exercises during pregnancy.
Bleeding, leaking fluid, chest pain, dizziness or painful contractions during exercise: stop and get checked.
With conditions such as placenta praevia or a risk of preterm birth, ask your doctor before exercising.
Warning signs in pregnancy
Some symptoms need you to go to a health facility without waiting.
Early diagnosis can be vital for mother and baby.
These symptoms should be taken seriously at every stage of pregnancy.
Save the emergency contact details of the hospital where you will give birth in your phone.
Note the symptom, when it started and how long it lasted.
Vaginal bleeding or leaking fluid.
Severe or persistent tummy pain.
Severe headache, vision problems, sudden swelling of the face and hands.
A clear decrease in your baby's movements (in the last months).
High fever, shortness of breath, fainting, seizure: call your local emergency number.
Pre-eclampsia
A condition usually seen after week 20, with high blood pressure and effects on organs.
That's why blood pressure and a urine test are checked at every visit.
A first pregnancy, twins, chronic high blood pressure and kidney disease increase the risk.
If the risk is high, your doctor may recommend low-dose aspirin; don't take it on your own.
Don't miss check-ups; if you were asked to measure blood pressure at home, record it.
Watch for sudden weight gain and swelling.
Severe headache, flashing lights or blurred vision.
Pain in the upper right tummy or stomach, vomiting.
Sudden swelling of the face and hands, shortness of breath: get help right away.
Gestational diabetes
High blood sugar that appears in pregnancy and usually goes away after birth.
It is screened with a glucose tolerance test between weeks 24 and 28.
If not controlled, it can lead to a large baby and a difficult birth.
Women who had gestational diabetes have a higher risk of type 2 diabetes later.
Follow the dietitian's advice; limit sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates.
Short walks after meals help regulate blood sugar.
Record your blood sugar readings; have the follow-up test after birth.
If readings are consistently above target.
Extreme thirst, weeing often, blurred vision.
Baby's movements
A change in your baby's movement pattern is an important health sign.
In a first pregnancy movements are usually felt at weeks 18–22, earlier in later pregnancies.
In the last months the type of movement changes, but the number should not decrease.
Your baby's own pattern matters more than any fixed "10 movements" count.
Pay attention every day at the times your baby is most active.
Lie on your left side in a quiet place and focus on the movements.
A clear decrease or change in movements: get checked the same day instead of drinking something cold and waiting.
Feeling no movement at all.
Medicines and supplements in pregnancy
Many medicines can be used safely in pregnancy, but every medicine and herbal product should be checked with a doctor.
Herbal teas and supplements may not be safe even if "natural".
Stopping medicines for chronic conditions on your own is also risky.
Some painkillers are not recommended at certain stages of pregnancy.
Take a list of all your medicines and supplements to your doctor.
Always tell your pharmacist you are pregnant.
If you took a medicine by mistake and are worried, ask your doctor; if you suspect poisoning, call your poison control centre.
Travel and daily life in pregnancy
In uncomplicated pregnancies, travel, work and sex can usually continue.
The most comfortable time to fly is usually weeks 14–28; airlines may ask for a medical certificate late in pregnancy.
The risk of blood clots increases on long journeys.
The seat belt should go below the bump and between the breasts.
On long journeys, walk every 1–2 hours and drink plenty of water.
Take your pregnancy notes and test results with you when travelling.
Talk to your doctor about travel to areas with infection risks such as Zika.
Swelling, pain and redness in one leg (it could be a clot).
Bleeding, leaking fluid or regular contractions while travelling.
Signs that labour is starting
Regular contractions that come closer together, waters breaking and a show can mean labour has started.
False (Braxton Hicks) contractions are irregular and ease with rest.
Real labour contractions are regular and get stronger and closer together.
Labour usually lasts longer with a first baby.
Note when contractions start and how far apart they are.
Go to hospital when your doctor advised (for example, when contractions come every 5 minutes, last 1 minute and continue for 1 hour).
If your waters break, note the colour and the time.
Waters breaking (especially green, brown or foul-smelling).
Heavy bleeding, constant and severe tummy pain.
Fewer baby movements.
Regular contractions before week 37 (preterm labour).
Packing the bag in weeks 34–36 avoids last-minute rush.
Hospitals provide some items; find out your hospital's list.
For mum: ID, pregnancy notes and test results, front-opening nightgown, nursing bra, maternity pads, slippers, charger.
For baby: 2–3 sets of vests and sleepsuits, hat, socks, blanket, newborn nappies.
For going home: weather-appropriate clothes and a rear-facing car seat.
Snacks and spare clothes for your support person.
Vaginal birth and caesarean section
How you give birth is planned with your doctor according to your and your baby's condition.
A vaginal birth usually means faster recovery.
A caesarean is life-saving when medically needed; as major surgery, recovery takes longer.
A vaginal birth after a previous caesarean may be possible under the right conditions.
Discuss your birth preferences and questions with your doctor in advance.
Antenatal classes help you learn breathing and relaxation techniques.
If signs of labour start before the planned date, go to your hospital.
Pain relief in labour
There are many drug-free and medical ways to cope with labour pain.
An epidural is a common method, given in the lower back, that greatly reduces pain.
Breathing techniques, moving, a warm shower and having a support person make it easier to cope.
Find out the options and what your hospital offers in advance.
Tell the team clearly what you need during labour.
The first hour after birth: skin-to-skin contact
Skin-to-skin contact right after birth and breastfeeding in the first hour bring many benefits to mother and baby.
Skin-to-skin contact regulates your baby's temperature and heartbeat and makes it easier to start breastfeeding.
Colostrum (first milk) comes in small amounts but is very valuable.
It is often possible after a caesarean too.
Tell the birth team your wishes in advance.
In the first hour, give your baby the chance to find the breast.
The postpartum period
The first 6 weeks after birth are when your body recovers and you need rest and support most.
Postpartum bleeding (lochia) can last 4–6 weeks; it gradually lessens and becomes lighter.
Uterine cramps may be felt, especially while breastfeeding.
The postnatal check-up is usually at 6 weeks; earlier checks may also be recommended.
Rest while your baby sleeps; ask for help with housework.
Drink plenty and eat a balanced diet; ask your doctor about iron supplements.
Go to your check-ups; write down your questions.
Bleeding that soaks a pad every hour, or large clots.
Foul-smelling discharge, fever, increasing tummy pain.
Swelling/pain in one leg, chest pain or shortness of breath: emergency.
Severe headache or vision problems (could be postpartum pre-eclampsia).
Caring for stitches and a caesarean wound
Stitches after birth usually heal in a few weeks; hygiene and rest support healing.
Episiotomy stitches mostly dissolve on their own.
Full recovery after a caesarean can take 6–8 weeks.
After using the toilet, rinse front to back with lukewarm water and pat dry.
Change pads often.
After a caesarean avoid heavy lifting; support your tummy with a pillow when coughing.
Use painkillers as your doctor advises.
Redness, discharge, opening or increasing pain at the wound.
Fever.
Breastfeeding basics
Exclusive breast milk for the first 6 months, then breastfeeding alongside solid foods up to 2 years and beyond is recommended.
The colostrum of the first days is little but enough; milk usually increases on day 2–5.
With a good latch, your baby's mouth is wide open, lips turned out and most of the dark area around the nipple is in the mouth.
Milk production follows demand: the more often you feed, the more milk is made.
Feed on demand, at least 8–12 times a day.
Let your baby finish one breast before offering the other.
Track wet and dirty nappies; add feeding entries in the app.
If you are struggling, get support from a breastfeeding counsellor or health facility.
If your baby doesn't have enough wet nappies or isn't gaining weight.
Redness, hardness in the breast, fever (could be mastitis).
Nipple cracks that don't heal, bleeding or severe pain.
Worrying about low milk supply
Many mothers worry their milk isn't enough; usually it is and the baby grows well.
Softer breasts and frequent feeding don't mean low supply.
During growth spurts (2–3 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months) your baby may want to feed more often.
Topping up with bottles and formula can lower milk production by reducing how often you breastfeed.
Feed more often; do skin-to-skin contact.
Expressing after feeds can increase production.
Drink enough and rest.
Decide with a health professional whether top-ups are needed.
Fewer than 6 wet nappies a day after day 5.
Your baby not getting back to birth weight in 2 weeks or not gaining weight.
Expressing and storing milk
Expressed breast milk keeps its nutritional value when stored correctly.
Fresh milk keeps about 4 hours at room temperature (up to 25 °C), 4 days in the fridge and about 6 months (up to 12) in the freezer.
Thawed milk should be used within 24 hours in the fridge and not refrozen.
Milk left over after your baby has drunk from it should be used within 2 hours or thrown away.
Wash your hands before expressing; clean pump parts after every use.
Store milk in small portions, labelled with the date.
Thaw in the fridge or in lukewarm water; don't use a microwave.
Breast engorgement and mastitis
Overfull breasts and blocked milk ducts can cause pain and sometimes infection (mastitis).
With mastitis there is a red, hot, painful area on the breast and flu-like symptoms.
Continuing to breastfeed usually helps recovery and doesn't harm the baby.
Feed or express often; start your baby on the painful breast.
A cold compress after feeding may ease swelling.
Avoid tight bras and lying on your front.
Use painkillers and fever reducers after asking a doctor.
Fever and chills, or pain or redness that doesn't improve in 24 hours.
A lump or a feeling of pus collecting in the breast.
Sore and cracked nipples
Nipple pain during breastfeeding is mostly caused by latch problems and can be fixed.
Mild tenderness in the first days is normal; ongoing pain is not.
A tongue-tie can make latching harder for some babies.
Fix the latch: bring your baby to the breast tummy to tummy, nose level with the nipple.
After feeding, rub a few drops of milk on the nipple and let it dry.
Creams containing lanolin can be used.
Break the suction with your finger when taking your baby off the breast.
Bleeding cracks, white patches or burning (could be thrush).
If the pain gets worse with each feed or your baby isn't gaining weight.
Pelvic floor and recovery after birth
Pregnancy and birth can weaken the pelvic floor muscles; exercises can strengthen them.
Urine leakage after birth is common and can often be treated.
Separation of the tummy muscles (diastasis) can lessen over time with suitable exercise.
Do pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises regularly every day.
Wait for your postnatal check-up before starting strenuous exercise.
Start with walking and build up slowly.
Urine or wind leakage that continues months after birth.
A feeling of prolapse or heaviness in the vagina.
Contraception after birth
You can get pregnant even before your first period after birth.
Breastfeeding alone gives temporary protection only under certain conditions (baby under 6 months, exclusive breastfeeding, no periods).
Oestrogen-free methods are preferred for breastfeeding mothers.
Discuss the options with your doctor at the postnatal check-up.
The menstrual cycle
The menstrual cycle is the time from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.
In adults a cycle of 21–35 days is considered normal.
Period bleeding usually lasts 2–7 days.
Ovulation usually happens about 14 days before the next period.
Record the days your period starts in the app's calendar; your average cycle is calculated.
Note pain, discharge and mood changes in the women's health journal.
Cycles consistently shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days.
No period for more than 3 months (once pregnancy is ruled out).
Bleeding for more than 7 days or so heavy you change a pad every hour.
Bleeding between periods or after sex.
Period pain (dysmenorrhoea)
Period pain is common; if it is severe enough to affect daily life, it should be assessed.
Primary period pain is usually felt in the first 1–2 days of the period.
Severe pain that gets worse over the years can be a sign of conditions such as endometriosis.
Put a warm compress on your tummy and do light exercise.
Use painkillers according to the leaflet or your doctor's advice.
Record the severity and duration of the pain in your journal.
Pain that doesn't respond to painkillers or makes you miss school/work.
If there is pain during sex, irregular bleeding or fever.
Premenstrual syndrome (PMS)
Emotional and physical changes in the days before a period.
Bloating, breast tenderness, irritability, tiredness and appetite changes are common.
Symptoms usually ease once the period starts.
A severe form with marked depression and anger (PMDD) can be treated.
Record symptoms in your journal for 2–3 cycles.
Regular exercise, enough sleep and cutting down on salt and caffeine can help.
If symptoms seriously affect work and relationships.
Thoughts of harming yourself: get support right away (call your local emergency number).
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
A common hormonal condition with irregular periods, signs of excess androgens and many small follicles in the ovaries.
Irregular or infrequent periods, acne, excess hair and weight gain may occur.
It is linked to insulin resistance; lifestyle changes are an important part of treatment.
It can make getting pregnant harder, but there are treatment options.
Regular exercise and a balanced diet can reduce symptoms.
Record your period dates and take them to check-ups.
Very infrequent periods or none at all.
If you're planning a pregnancy, get assessed early.
Endometriosis
A condition, which can be painful, in which tissue similar to the womb lining grows outside the womb.
It can be linked to severe period pain, pain during sex and infertility.
Diagnosis can take years; taking symptoms seriously is important.
Record the severity and timing of the pain in your journal.
Discuss treatment options with a gynaecologist.
Pelvic pain that affects daily life.
Pain on opening the bowels or weeing during your period.
Smear, HPV and cervical cancer screening
Cervical cancer can largely be prevented with regular screening and the HPV vaccine.
In Türkiye's national programme, an HPV test and smear every 5 years are recommended for women aged 30–65.
Cancer screening centres (KETEM) and family health centres do screening.
The HPV vaccine is most effective when given before becoming sexually active.
Add your screening date to your calendar and to a reminder in the app.
Ask your doctor whether you are eligible for the HPV vaccine.
Bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods, foul-smelling discharge.
